---
title: "Wade In"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will choose how much of your data and your machine to hand over for one task, and start at the lowest step that gets the job done.
- **Before you start:** [Know Your Gear](know-your-gear.html), and Python 3 for the exercise. Your own data agreement overrides anything here.
- **Time:** about 20 minutes.
:::

## The scene

Two colleagues each have a report to write. A manager needs a status report across projects: which milestones are open and who is blocked, kept in a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets). A data analyst needs a count of samples received per project from the project database, using SQL (the language for querying a database). Both have two worries. The first is where the data goes. The second is a belief that to use an LLM at all they must let an agent loose on their computer.

Between "never" and "the agent runs my machine" there are several steps, and many useful tasks sit on the lower ones. You may stop at any step. Choosing not to climb is a legitimate decision at every one.

## Two dials

Two questions turn independently.

1. **What leaves your machine?** With a hosted model, anything you type, paste or upload is sent to the provider, and so is anything an agent reads. Claude Code sends all prompts and model outputs over the network. A model running on your own machine (a local model) keeps prompts local, though web or tool calls it makes may still reach out.
2. **What may the tool do?** It may only produce text. It may read files. It may edit files. It may run commands.

A chat window has the lowest second dial and can still carry a whole table to the provider if you paste one. A read-only agent has a low second dial too, and it still sends whatever it reads. Each dial needs its own decision.

## The ladder

| Step | What you do | What leaves | What the tool can do |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Do the work yourself | nothing | nothing |
| 1 | Chat with no data | the words you type | produce text |
| 2 | Chat with headings or schema and invented rows; you run the result | those names and the invented rows | produce text |
| 3 | A small extract your agreement allows, or a local model | the extract; nothing for a local model | produce text |
| 4 | A read-only agent on a copy of the data | everything it reads | read files |
| 5 | An agent that edits and runs commands | everything it reads, and more if what it runs sends it | change files, run commands |

Pasting the results of a step 2 task back into the chat sends those rows too, which makes it step 3.

What each step looks like for the two colleagues:

| Step | Manager: status report in a spreadsheet | Data analyst: samples in a database |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Build the status table by hand | Write the query and counts yourself |
| 1 | Ask for a report outline and wording for blockers | Ask how to explain a fall in sample numbers |
| 2 | Paste column headings and invented rows; apply the formula or pivot table yourself | Paste the schema only; run the query read-only yourself |
| 3 | Tidy blocker notes with a local model | Summarise free-text notes with a local model |
| 4 | Read-only agent on a copy of the workbook folder | Read-only agent on a copy of the database |
| 5 | Agent that edits the workbook or scripts and runs commands | Agent that edits and runs pipeline code |

A query that only reads is a SQL request that starts with SELECT. Plan mode is a mode where the agent reads and proposes and does not edit. It belongs to step 4: it limits what the agent does, while what is exposed depends on what it reads, and reading sends it. A copy of the data protects the original from edits and is still sent when read.

## Three questions before any step

1. **What kind of data is it?** The table gives a typical starting point. Your agreement, your data steward and your institution's rules decide, and they can be stricter.
2. **Which account will you use?** Consumer and organisation accounts have different terms, listed below.
3. **What leaves at this step?** Say it in one sentence before you press enter.

| Kind of data | Typical starting point |
|---|---|
| Public or already published | Any step |
| Internal, not personal (project names, milestone dates, status) | Steps 1 to 3 on an allowed account; 4 to 5 on an approved account, on a copy |
| Personal data, including pseudonymised codes | Steps 0 to 2 with no real rows; higher needs approval |
| Controlled or special-category data (health, genetic) | Steps 0 to 2; anything else only if your agreement says so in writing |

Pseudonymised codes replace names and still count as personal data. A data steward is the person at your organisation who looks after data rules; ask them about personal data. A local model is an option for controlled data only if your agreement allows that copy. Small counts can single people out even when no names are present, so check your policy before pasting results for rare groups.

## What a chat window keeps

- **Consumer accounts (Free, Pro, Max)** have a setting that lets chats improve the models. With it on, data may be kept, with identifying details removed, for up to 5 years.
- **Commercial accounts (such as Claude for Work and the API):** inputs and outputs are not used for training, with exceptions such as feedback you send. They are deleted from the provider's storage within 30 days by default, and kept longer for content flagged for a policy violation or when a longer-retention service is used.
- **Consumer accounts, after you delete a chat:** it leaves the provider's storage within 30 days.
- **Incognito chats** are not used for training. They are kept for 30 days by default, longer if an Enterprise organisation sets a longer period or if the chat is flagged for a policy violation.
- **People reading chats:** for consumer accounts, Anthropic staff cannot read conversations by default unless you share them as feedback. Designated members of a Trust and Safety team may access that data on a need-to-know basis.
- **Uploaded files, screenshots, images, chat memory, connectors and browsing:** treat each as data you share, like pasted text, and check how your tool handles it.
- **Other providers' chat tools** have their own terms. Read those for the tool you use.
- **To find out which account you are on,** look at the plan shown in your account settings, and ask your administrator if your organisation provides it. The training setting for consumer accounts sits in the privacy settings.

## Hands-on (data analyst): the samples count, without handing over the data

Files: [make_db.py](../../exercises/basecamp/wade-in/make_db.py), [run_query.py](../../exercises/basecamp/wade-in/run_query.py), [report-query.sql](../../exercises/basecamp/wade-in/report-query.sql) and [check-samples.sql](../../exercises/basecamp/wade-in/check-samples.sql). Save all four into an empty folder. Every row is invented. No LLM is called.

1. **Build the mock database and the schema text.** Run `python3 make_db.py` (or `python`, depending on your machine). It writes `mock.db` and `schema-only.txt`. Open the text file: table and column names, no rows. That is all that would go into a chat window at step 2. Look at the column names. `participant_code` and `notes` hint at what the real database holds, so decide whether even the names are fine to send.
2. **Write the prompt you would send.**

   ```text
   I have a SQLite database with this schema:
   <paste schema-only.txt>
   Write one read-only SQL query that gives, for each project, the number of
   samples received and the number of open milestones (done = 0).
   I will run it myself and check the numbers. Do not ask me to paste any rows.
   ```

3. **Read the reply.** `report-query.sql` stands in for what a model sent back. Read it before you run it: is it a single `SELECT`, and does it touch only the tables you expect? Then run `python3 run_query.py report-query.sql`. The script opens the database read-only, so a `DELETE` fails with "attempt to write a readonly database".
4. **Check it with a query the model did not write.** Run `python3 run_query.py check-samples.sql` and compare:

   | Project | Model's query: samples | Your check: samples | Model's query: open milestones | Open milestones in the data |
   |---|---|---|---|---|
   | Heron | 22 | 11 | 22 | 2 |
   | Kelp | 28 | 14 | 28 | 2 |
   | Vega | 34 | 17 | 34 | 2 |

   The query ran without an error, and its numbers are wrong. If you cannot run Python, read the table as a worked example, or ask a colleague to run it with you. Each project has two open milestones, and the query pairs every sample with every open milestone, so each sample is counted twice, and the milestone column repeats the same inflated number. Ask the model (or edit the query yourself) to fix it, then run both again until you get 11 and 2 for Heron.

The data stayed on your machine all the way through. Only the schema and the query text travelled. Running without an error and being right are separate questions, so the check against a second query matters.

## Hands-on (manager): the same check in a spreadsheet

The check is the same in a spreadsheet. At step 2 you paste only the column headings (for example Project, Milestone, Owner, Status, Blocked by) and two or three invented rows, and ask for a formula or pivot table that counts open milestones per project. You apply it to your real sheet yourself.

Then check it against something the model did not write. Use `COUNTIF` to count the rows per project and compare with the model's formula. With invented numbers: if each of three projects has 6 milestone rows and the model's formula shows 18 for every project, it counted the whole column instead of one project's rows. Find out why the two differ before you put either number in the report.

## Climbing, if and when you want to

- Move up a step when you have a task the lower step could not do, and a sentence saying what leaves.
- Before steps 4 and 5, work on a **copy** of the data, set a save point and add permission rules.
- For sensitive data you may prefer to stay on a local model, when your agreement allows that copy.
- If you have already pasted something you should not have, stop and tell your data steward.
- A one-line message for your data steward: "For a report from the project database I want to use [tool, account type] at step [n]. What leaves is [what]. Is that allowed for [data kind]?"

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Is my data used for model training? (consumer)](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023580-is-my-data-used-for-model-training): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is the page that says the training setting exists for Free, Pro and Max chats, which decides your first account question.
- [How long do you store my data?](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023548-how-long-do-you-store-my-data): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it gives the 5-year and 30-day figures for consumer chats and what happens after you delete one.
- [How long do you store my organization's data?](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996866-how-long-do-you-store-my-organization-s-data): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is the commercial-account counterpart, with the 30-day default and the cases that keep data longer.
- [Use incognito chats](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12260368-use-incognito-chats): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows what incognito does and does not change, so you do not over-trust the name.
- [Data usage (Claude Code)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it states that the agent sends prompts and outputs over the network, which is what makes steps 4 and 5 different from running a query yourself.
- [Ollama FAQ](https://docs.ollama.com/faq): Ollama, docs. Why read: it says local runs do not send prompts to Ollama and separates its cloud models, which matters if you choose a local model for sensitive data.
- [AI for Science: the short version](https://aiforscience.eu/short-version/): AI for Science, article. Why read: a one-page European draft summary of research practices, useful for a conversation with your data steward. It is a draft without endorsements.
:::
